newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli stocks look good despite slowing economy.
newsitem.headline: Israeli stocks look good despite slowing economy.

text.p: Israel's economy is slowing and Middle East peace is on shaky ground, but analysts say the Tel Aviv stock market should begin recovering in 1997 after a three-year slump -- and it might turn into a bull run.
"The stock market will be positive next year, even if there are some negative conditions," said Doron Tsur, head of research of Sahar Securities.
Like other analysts, he is counting on the government's plans to slash the budget by some 6.1 billion shekels in 1997 and rein in the deficit.

If the government succeeds, the Bank of Israel is expected to lower short-term interest rates over the next quarter by about 1.5 percentage points from the current 15.2 percent. A depreciation of the Israeli shekel, now widely seen as overvalued, should follow.

Eli Nahum, head of trading at Zannex Securities, is confident the chain of events will occur and said the Tel Aviv market is already rallying in anticipation. Since early November, the benchmark Mishtanim index has risen 10.5 percent.

"I think (the bull market) has already started. Technically, something has changed in the market in the last three or four weeks," Nahum said, citing increased trading volume and the rally in small-capitalisation shares.
Redemptions in the mutual and provident funds, which have drained the market of capital, have fallen to nearly nil.
Even analysts who are less sanguine about the market's prospects still believe the outlook is good.

"We could be on the threshold of a bull market, but we could be on a threshold for another six months," warned an analyst for a U.S. brokerage. "There are still a lot of things that need to be in place before a rally."
But, she added: "I think the market will perform much better in 1997."

Even if government spending is cut and interest rates fall, Israel's economy is likely to post a second year of relatively slow growth in 1997. Gross domestic product is expected to grow only 3.8 percent this year, down from 7.1 percent in 1995. The government is forecasting four percent growth in 1997.
That is why analysts are focusing on export-oriented companies, mainly in chemicals and high technology, which will benefit from the expected weakening of the shekel.
There are a few high-tech shares traded in Tel Aviv, together with high-tech holding companies like Clal Electronic Industries, but most of the sector is traded on Nasdaq.

Analysts are also looking favourably on bank stocks, especially Bank Leumi. The shares are cheap and the banks have made large numbers of foreign-currency linked loans in the last two years whose value rises as the shekel weakens, said Tsur.
"Once the market turns optimistic, the bank sector will outperform," Nahum said.

Because of the economic slowdown, most analysts are shying away from the retail sector, with the exception of supermarkets. "Retail food sales are still growing rapidly. New supermarkets are being developed in urban areas," said the U.S. analyst.
But Tsur contends that many other domestic plays can be a good bet in the slowing economy.

Many Israeli companies saw their domestic sales pounded by the overvalued shekel, which allowed cheap imports to flood the market. A weaker shekel will let them win back market share, while lower interest rates will help earnings, Nahum said.
"We have been in a period of declining profitability (since the end of 1992), but I think we're at the end of the cycle," he said.

Analysts are also looking at restructuring plays, like Elite Industries and Clal Israel, both of which are under new management. Indeed, after a three-year market slump, said analysts, it is hard to find Israeli stocks that are not selling very cheaply.

It is difficult to find an analyst bullish about the future of the Middle East peace process, but most do not think the right-wing policies of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will cause lasting damage.

"People are getting used to the (new) government, although there are a lot of uncertainties," said the U.S. analyst. She maintains that foreign investors will stay warm to Israel so long as they perceive movement in the peace process.
